About the artist: Jesus Miguel Avena is a Mestizo, Queer Mexican American oil painter and ceramicist based in Santa Fe, New Mexico. His work explores identity, embodiment, and cultural hybridity through visual storytelling informed by Mesoamerican mythologies, Indigenous philosophies, and the concept of Nepantla — an in between space of transformation. Moving between painting and clay, Avena creates figurative works and ceramic objects that examine memory and layered Mexican American histories. He earned degrees from Santa Fe Community College (2022) and the Institute of American Indian Arts (IAIA,2024). Avena has exhibited nationally, participated in the Venice Biennale through an IAIA–Marist partnership, and currently serves as Visiting Assistant Professor of Ceramics at IAIA while preparing to pursue an MFA.

Film Screening: Eco Docs- The River That Harms

Sunday, October 4 2026
1:30 pm Paul Pino Opening Performance 
2:00 pm Film Begins

NHCC | Bank of America Theatre

NHCC presents a series of documentaries about environmental hardships from the Southwest throughout Latin America. These matinee film screenings pair perfectly with a visit to the Visual Arts Museum before or after. Explore the subject matter of environmental justice through multiple mediums in one afternoon.

The River That Harms, Directed & Produced by Colleen Ann Keane, documents the largest radioactive wastewater spill in United States history, a national tragedy that took place on the Navajo Nation.

In 1979, a United Nuclear Corporation tailings dam at Church Rock, New Mexico, collapsed, releasing 94 million gallons of radioactive wastewater and uranium mill waste into the Rio Puerco. The contaminated water flowed through Diné communities where the river served as a vital source of water for families, livestock, and farmland. Through interviews and firsthand testimony, The River That Harms documents the devastating environmental and human consequences of uranium extraction on Navajo land and preserves the voices and experiences of those directly impacted by the Church Rock uranium spill. More than four decades later, the film remains an urgent warning about the ongoing consequences of nuclear extraction and environmental contamination.

A performance by Paul Pino will open the event.

event.description:
Herencia Speaker Series: Faith and Resilience

Saturday, October 10, 2026,
10:00 am (Film) & 11:00 (Presentation)
NHCC | Salón Ortega

Head to the Center for a presentation by Cecilia Navarrete and Anthony DellaFlora on the centuries-old reverence for La Virgen de Guadalupe and the lives built around the Albuquerque’s historic railyard.

10:00am
Fiestas of Our Lady of Guadalupe:
A Century of Veneration
by Anthony DellaFlora

Anthony DellaFlora began his award-winning documentary film career more than 25 years ago as producer of the cult classic High Strange New Mexico, an independent production about the state’s UFO subculture. Since then, he has produced dozens of documentaries for PBS, GOV-TV and the city’s Public Art program on a variety of subjects including the Balloon Fiesta, Open Space, the National Senior Games, Breaking Bad, volcanoes, Native American cosmology, public art projects, and the federal judicial system.

11:00am
Forged in Diversity: Albuquerque Railyard Workers (1880-1950)
by Cecilia Navarrete

Cecilia Navarrete is a native New Mexican who partnered with William Brown of the Wheels Museum to research the lives of Albuquerque railyards workers. Drawing on historical records, their work highlights the contributions of New Mexico Hispanos and Mexican immigrants to the railroad industry and Albuquerque’s growth. A former educator, researcher, and consultant with a Ph.D. from Stanford University, Cecilia brings more than 45 years of experience to preserving and sharing New Mexico history.

Opera Southwest Presents: The New Mexico Symphonic Chorus with the Opera Southwest Orchestra

In 1850, Berlioz slipped a gentle chorus into a Paris concert and credited it to “Pierre Ducré,” a 17th-century church composer he’d invented outright. Parisians who couldn’t stand his music were charmed: one declared that “Berlioz could never write a tune so beautiful”. He spent the next four years building a full oratorio around that little piece: L’Enfance du Christ, tracing the Holy Family’s flight into Egypt across three parts and ninety minutes. Most people know only its one famous excerpt, “The Shepherds’ Farewell”; the complete work is rarely performed, which makes hearing the whole of it a real occasion.

Featuring John Tiranno, Javier Ortiz, Cecilia Violetta López, and Ashraf Sewailam, conducted by Zoe Zeniodi.

Zappa’s virtuosity on the guitar is matched only by his prolific compositional skills, which have generated numerous original works spanning multiple albums including “Confessions of Deprived Youth” (1991) and “Via Zammata” (2015). Notably, his compositions have even been performed by a 100-piece orchestra in Holland, showcasing his versatility and command of orchestral arrangements. His music effortlessly traverses genres, seamlessly weaving together elements of rock, fusion, and experimental sounds, all while maintaining a signature style that is unmistakably his own. In addition to his solo work, Dweezil has collaborated with an impressively varied roster of artists, including Edward Van Halen, Deep Purple, Lisa Loeb, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock and Steve Vai, among others.

In 2020, Dweezil further solidified his reputation as a pioneer in the industry by completing construction on “Hikari,” a state-of-the-art multimedia studio. As a sought-after audio mix engineer, he showcased his expertise by crafting the stereo and Atmos mixes for the 50th anniversary re-release of Deep Purple’s legendary album “Machine Head” in 2024, cementing his status as a unique voice in sound engineering.

Beyond his artistic pursuits, Dweezil is deeply passionate about music education. He frequently shares his knowledge and expertise by teaching guitar, both through his own music camp, “Dweezilla,” and online lessons. His collaborative spirit has led him to work with a diverse array of musicians all while honoring the legacy of his father, Frank Zappa.

In all his endeavors, Dweezil remains committed to upholding integrity and pushing the boundaries of technology and creativity. As he continues to innovate and inspire, Dweezil Zappa stands as a true luminary in the world of music and beyond.

About the artist: Joe Ramiro Garcia is an Art Institute of Chicago–educated artist who moved to Santa Fe from his native Houston in 1987. In his paintings, he creates an image or pattern on paper that’s soaked in gum arabic and water, next the paper plate is charged with oil paint and then hand pressed onto a painting surface. It’s a transfer method similar to those used by Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol, and Nancy Spero—but also vastly different, because Garcia doesn’t silkscreen, monoprint, or etch. The end results are oil paintings that Garcia calls “open narratives” due to layered imagery. Garcia, who is represented by Blue Gallery in Kansas City, has recently had several solo exhibitions at Santa Fe’s LewAllen Galleries.

About the artist: Esteban Ismael Durán, a self-taught artist, was born in 1955 and grew up in Albuquerque’s historic Old Town. His roots in that traditional community have always been important to him and helped him to shape his work. As a young man, he began his formal studies with artist Frank McCulloch. In 1993 he started incorporating traditional New Mexican tinwork into his paintings, studying this discipline with tinsmith Ted Arellanes. Esteban’s local work has included public art for the City of Albuquerque and Bernalillo County. He, along with his cousin PAZ, had the lead role in the 1995 creation of a series of tile murals along Fourth Street in Barelas, mentoring local youth to help design the murals based on Barelas’ history. Esteban began to work with recycled materials as he ventured into combining traditional tinwork with more contemporary media. For the past ten years, he has built the unique ability to blend contemporary and traditional media/design and the use of recycled materials.

Join us for a poetry workshop with writer Leticia Urieta. The body carries our stories, but sometimes delving into these stories can be difficult and painful to navigate. We have to engage in acts of radical and deep reflection to fully embody and write about the traumas, beauty, pain and healing that our bodies are capable of holding.

This generative workshop will ask you to engage in these acts of radical reflection to explore your relationships to the body through free writing, poetry and creative nonfiction. We will explore how writers embody their experiences through poetry and prose by studying contemporary poets and writers who are engaging with discussions about the body and chronic illness, pain, trauma and healing. Participants will be given the opportunity to generate new work as well as to engage with their own work (or ideas) in progress. Author, poet, and teaching artist, Leticia Urieta, will be joining us at the NHCC to share her new poetry book, Offerings to a Tumbled Temple. In this stunning poetry collection, Urieta transforms the lived experience of chronic pain and healing into ritual, language, and myth. The body—both sacred and wounded—becomes the site of prayer and reckoning. Through altars built of blood, memory, and tenderness, these poems offer not only lamentation but also fierce reclamation: the body as temple, tumbled yet enduring. 

Drawing inspiration from writers such as Sonya Huber, Ada Limón, and Torrin A. Greathouse, Urieta writes toward acceptance and reclamation. Offerings to a Tumbled Temple is a testament to survival and love in all its painful forms—a book that insists on the beauty of the body’s resilience.
